whyCorrect: The claim has a comparison built into it: the relationship is more strained than it once was, so the quotation must show both the present friction and the warmer past. This one does. The professor is ordering Vanya out of the room — present conflict — and appeals to "our former friendship," which marks that friendship as something now behind them.

whyWrong.B: Vanya's complaint that he was never thanked "neither in my youth nor now" describes a grievance that has held the whole time, so it shows no worsening.
whyWrong.C: Vanya mocking the professor's self-pity shows current contempt but gives no picture of an earlier state.
whyWrong.D: The professor's irritation with how others treat him is present-tense resentment with nothing to compare it against.

tips: When a claim says "more X than it once was," reject any quotation that shows only the present.

whyCorrect: Trace the mechanism the passage gives. Water evaporating from the crust leaves voids, and oil — a pure fat — fills those voids. Less moisture lost therefore means fewer voids, and fewer voids mean less oil taken up. So low-moisture-loss sections end up with less fat.

whyWrong.A: Crust thickness is never linked to moisture loss in the passage; the described consequence of evaporation is voids that fill with oil.
whyWrong.C: The text says water keeps migrating outward as long as the crust stays permeable, but it never says how much moisture is lost determines when permeability ends.
whyWrong.D: Final temperature is not part of the described process at all.

commonMistakes: Stopping at "less water lost" without carrying the chain through to the voids and the oil that replaces them.

whyCorrect: Contemporary painters like Hardridge build compositions from motifs specific to their tribes, so the Indigenous character is visible in the style itself. West's generation instead worked in Abstract Expressionism, a school dominated by European American artists, rather than in traditional Indigenous nonrepresentational forms. With nothing distinctive in the style to point to, calling their work Indigenous art rests on knowing who made it.

whyWrong.A: The passage does not deny cultural identity's influence; it says the influence is not legible in these paintings' style.
whyWrong.C: There is no claim that Abstract Expressionist motifs have Indigenous origins.
whyWrong.D: Aesthetic merit is never discussed, so no trade-off between biography and merit is on the table.

tips: "Thus" means the completion must follow from the contrast just drawn — style-based identification versus artist-based identification.

whyCorrect: Read all the way to the end of the sentence: the main verb is "analyzed geotagged social media posts." The subject "a team of researchers" already has its verb, so the blank cannot supply a second finite verb. It has to be a participial phrase describing the team, which is "hoping to find connections ..."

whyWrong.A: "Were hoping" is a finite verb, leaving two main verbs with no conjunction between them.
whyWrong.B: "Was hoping" has the same problem, and it is also singular.
whyWrong.C: "Hoped" likewise gives the sentence a second finite verb.

commonMistakes: Stopping at the blank; the long modifier hides the real verb "analyzed" until the end of the sentence.

whyCorrect: Both halves are complete sentences: Churchrock Chapter is one of the Navajo Nation's 110 chapters, and in Diné bizaad the chapter is called Kin Łitsoth Sínílí. A period is needed to separate them, with "In" opening the second. Notice that the second half already has its own comma after the parenthetical language name.

whyWrong.A: A comma between two independent clauses is a splice.
whyWrong.C: With no punctuation, "of the Navajo Nation in Diné bizaad" runs together and then collides with the second clause.
whyWrong.D: "And" alone cannot join the clauses without a comma before it, and it also attaches "in Diné bizaad" to the wrong half.

tips: Check whether the words after the blank form their own sentence — here they do, so the blank needs a full stop.

whyCorrect: "Okinaka doesn't make such decisions single-handedly, however" is one complete sentence, with "however" tacked on at the end and set off by the comma already in the passage. "All historical designations must be approved by a group of nine other experts" is a second complete sentence. A period between them is what separates two independent clauses.

whyWrong.B: "However and all" strings a conjunctive adverb into a conjunction and leaves the two clauses improperly joined.
whyWrong.C: With no punctuation after "however," the second clause runs straight on.
whyWrong.D: A comma after "however" joins two independent clauses with only a comma, which is a splice.

tips: "However" at the end of a clause is an adverb, not a joiner — it cannot hold two sentences together.
